vignette: He stands at the edge of the steel-framing crew when the warning sound cuts through the morning air. It is not a horn. It is the high-pitched shriek of a failing cable. Before anyone can shout, the scaffold buckles. He watches the way the metal groans, the sudden drop, then the terrible, muffled crack as Marcus goes down beneath a tangle of planks and rebar. The world narrows to the sound of Marcus's breathing, then nothing. He drops to his knees, fingers pressing against the cold steel beam, feeling the vibrations of the site fade into a ringing silence. The paramedics pull the body away two hours later. He does not remember the ride to the hospital. He only remembers the weight of his own hands, clean and useless. He tries to return to the trade. He straps on his tool belt, nails a stud, pours coffee from a dented thermos. But the rhythm of the site fractures. Every clang of a hammer sends a jolt through his chest. He starts arriving early, walking the perimeter of every foundation, checking tie-downs that have already been signed off by safety inspectors. His foreman notices the hesitation, the way he steps back when heavy loads are being lifted. He stops attending the Saturday shifters, cancels the crew barbecue, stops returning phone calls. His marriage unravels in the quiet spaces between his flinches. When his ex-wife tries to talk about the future, he hears the echo of the cable snap. He stops sleeping in the same room. The divorce papers arrive while he is tightening a bolt, the sound of the ratchet mirroring the snap in his head. His ex-wife's name still lives in his contacts, but he never scrolls to it. The silence between them has become a structure he lives inside. Three years later, he sits across from you in a sunlit office, but his eyes track the door, the ceiling, the ventilation grate. He speaks in low, measured sentences, each one carefully placed like a stone. He describes the nights when the house settles and he wakes gasping, heart hammering against his ribs, convinced the floor is giving way. He has learned to sleep on the bathroom floor, where the concrete feels stable. He avoids commercial job sites with exposed scaffolding, takes on only residential remodels where the materials feel familiar. He wears his hard hat now like armor, checking every beam twice, every bolt three times. The work no longer feels like building. It feels like holding back a collapse that has already happened. When a delivery truck backfires on the street outside, his shoulders hike to his ears and his breath stops. He tells you about the way his hands have lost their certainty. They tremble when he holds a coffee cup. They refuse to touch his daughter's shoulder, as if contact might transmit the fall. He goes to the grocery store early on Sundays. He counts the exits. He watches the people in the aisle not for threats, but for weight distribution, for the way shelves bow, for the tension in a ceiling joint. He is thirty-nine now, and the physical labor of construction has become a strange comfort, because the variables are known, even when his nervous system is not. He carries the weight of Marcus's last breath in his jaw, in his shoulders, in the tight rope that runs from his sternum to his throat. He does not know how to stop counting the beams. He only knows that when the wind shifts and the metal sings, he will be ready. He sits here, and he waits for the sound.
